identity.title: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action Models are Surprisingly Resistant to Forgetting in Continual Learning

problem.claim: Robot policies must learn new skills over time without catastrophically forgetting prior skills.

gap.claim: Continual learning in modern pretrained Vision-Language-Action models is underexplored relative to small behavior-cloning models trained from scratch.

contributions.claim: Pretrained VLAs are reported to be more resistant to forgetting than smaller policies trained from scratch.
Simple Experience Replay is reported to work well for VLAs, sometimes yielding zero forgetting with a small replay dataset.
The authors link pretraining to reduced forgetting, preserved forward learning, retention of prior-task knowledge, and rapid recovery through finetuning.

stated_novelty.claim: The work presents insights that large-scale pretraining changes continual-learning dynamics, allowing ongoing skill acquisition with simple replay.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that pretrained VLAs are remarkably resistant to forgetting compared with smaller from-scratch policy models.
The authors report that Experience Replay sometimes achieves zero forgetting on VLAs even with a small replay data size.
The authors report that retained prior-task knowledge enables rapid recovery of seemingly forgotten skills through finetuning.

narrative_sequence.summary: Continual robot policy learning requires acquiring skills without losing earlier ones.
Existing continual-learning study has focused mainly on small from-scratch behavior-cloning policies, leaving pretrained VLAs less explored.
Pretrained VLAs are reported to forget less than smaller from-scratch policies, and simple replay can sometimes eliminate forgetting with little data.

Pretraining is reported to support both low forgetting with small replay buffers and strong forward learning; prior knowledge may persist despite temporary performance decline and can be rapidly recovered by finetuning.
The authors interpret these results as evidence that large-scale pretraining changes continual-learning dynamics and supports continued skill acquisition with simple replay.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates observed forgetting from retained prior-task knowledge and subsequent recovery through finetuning.

lessons.interpretation: This framing distinguishes behavioral performance loss from loss of internal task knowledge.
lessons.application: When reporting continual-learning results, measure both immediate task performance and post-finetuning recovery to distinguish erasure from temporary interference.
lessons.exception: This move is unsuitable when recovery finetuning is not defined or when the study cannot assess prior-task representations or performance.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify tasks, model sizes, replay-buffer sizes, baselines, metrics, or experimental protocols.
The conditions under which zero forgetting occurs and the evidence for retained knowledge are not detailed.
The abstract does not quantify the speed or extent of recovery through finetuning.
